title: I will surely go with thee (Judges 4:6–10)
hookLine: Barak won't go into battle without her, and she goes

lines: IF THOU WILT GO WITH ME, I WILL GO.
cards: "If thou wilt go with me, then I will go: but if thou wilt not go with me, then I will not go." That's a soldier talking, to a judge. His name is Barak, son of Abinoam, and he's just been handed a war.
Deborah has sent for him from Kedesh in Naphtali.
The Lord has commanded, she tells him: gather ten thousand men from Naphtali and Zebulun at Mount Tabor, and Sisera and his chariots will be drawn to you at the river Kishon.
Barak hears all of it, and puts one condition on the table: you.

teach.b: Notice how Deborah delivers the call. She doesn't say, I've decided. She asks: hasn't the Lord, the God of Israel, commanded you?
As if Barak already knows, and needs someone to say it out loud. Barak's answer has been read in very different ways.

Some readers hear fear, or a lack of faith: the Lord promised victory, and he still wants a person beside him. Others hear something wiser: he won't go without the prophet, the one through whom the word came.

teach.h: FEAR, OR WISDOM? THE TEXT DOESN'T SAY.
teach.b: The text doesn't decide. What it shows is Deborah's answer, and it's short. No lecture.
No be brave, go alone. Just this: "I will surely go with thee." Then, in the same breath, an honest cost.

teach.h: INTO THE HAND OF A WOMAN.
teach.b: The journey won't be for your honor, she says, "for the LORD shall sell Sisera into the hand of a woman." Which woman? Some readers assume Deborah.
The text doesn't say, not yet.

teach.h: AND DEBORAH WENT UP WITH HIM.
teach.b: Then the plain line that ends the scene: Barak calls up Zebulun and Naphtali, ten thousand men go up behind him, "and Deborah went up with him." She had a tree, a court, a life where people came to her.
She leaves it to walk beside the man who asked her to come, toward an army of iron chariots. She doesn't fight for him. She doesn't shame him.

how: Jews read Deborah and Barak's story in Judges 4, and the exchange between them is discussed in commentary, with readers differing over whether Barak's condition shows weakness or faith in the prophet.

s: Deborah refused and told Barak to go alone
her answer was I will surely go with thee, and she went up with him.
Deborah said the honor would go to a woman
the Lord shall sell Sisera into the hand of a woman; the text doesn't yet say which.

it gives only his condition; readers differ on whether it was fear or wisdom.

games.q: you're Deborah. Barak says he'll go to war only if you come with him. what do you do?
o: tell him to trust God and go alone.
go with him, and tell him the honor won't be his.
games.why: I will surely go with thee, she says, but the Lord will sell Sisera into the hand of a woman. and Deborah went up with him.

practice: Bring to mind someone facing something hard soon, a doctor's appointment, an exam, a difficult conversation, a first day, and picture them asking quietly, will you come? Notice your first reaction, whatever it is.
Then picture what going could look like in real life: sitting in the waiting room, a call before and after, a message that morning.

wordCard.voice: Barak. The soldier who told Deborah he wouldn't go to war without her, and her short, surprising answer: I will surely go with thee. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: going, I will go, the doubled verb of Judges 4:9 that the KJV renders I will surely go.

carryVoice: Your line: I will go with you. Sometimes the answer is simply to come along. Day seven hundred thirteen.
